CITATION
:
Seed v. Desai, 2014 ONSC 3329

COURT FILE NO.:
FC-08-776-1

DATE:

20140516

ONTARIO

SUPERIOR COURT OF JUSTICE

BETWEEN:

)

)

Corie Seed

Applicant

– and –

Ebrahim Desai

Respondent

)

) )

Peter F. Burnet, for the Applicant

D. Larry Segal, for the Respondent

)

HEARD:
November 25 – 29, December 2 – 6, 9 – 11, 2013

REASONS
FOR JUDGMENT

J. MACKINNON J.

[
1
]

The parties separated in 2007.  In November 2010,
they settled parenting issues and consented to a final Order which did not
include any reference to legal custody, or decision making authority for the
children.  One of the important terms of the final Order was the appointment of
a parenting coordinator to help with dispute resolution.  This did not occur
and the case came back before the court in June 2011.  Now the mother seeks
sole custody and a continuation of the existing residential arrangements
whereby the children’s primary residence is with her.  She says the conflict
between her and the children’s father is so extreme that only one parent should
make decisions for the children.  For his part, the father also seeks sole
custody.  He proposes that the children alternate weekly between their parents’
homes.

[
2
]

The respondent’s income, child and spousal support
are also in issue.

Overview

[
3
]

The parties commenced cohabitation in August
1997.  They married on August 12, 2001 and separated on May 25, 2007.  They
have two daughters, Laila, who will turn eleven on June 7, and Maya, who is now
10 years old.  The parties were divorced in April 2010.

[
4
]

Their first court action was commenced in 2008.
In 2010, a final Order was issued with respect to property.  The property settlement
provided that the respondent kept the matrimonial home and assumed the two
encumbrances against it.  He paid $85,000 to the applicant for her interest in
the home.  The only other terms related to vehicles.  A final Order was also
issued on consent with respect to custody and access.  The parenting settlement
was reached on the eve of trial.  It provided primary residence to the
applicant mother with access to the respondent father.  He was entitled to have
the children with him alternate weekends and an overnight visit in the other
weeks.  Communications were limited to email, no more than two emails each
week.  There were additional terms with respect to holidays, birthdays, and
telephone access.  In addition, the parents agreed to obtain counselling for
their daughters and to retain a parenting coordinator to work with them in an
effort to improve their parenting relationship and to reduce the conflict
between them.  As noted, this final Order expressly made no award of custody to
either parent.

[
5
]

The parenting coordination never occurred.  The
respondent would not sign the coordinator’s standard form contract.  There was
no improvement in the parents’ relationship.  The father contacted the mother
much more frequently than permitted by the court  Order.  She says there have
been hundreds and hundreds of emails since the final Order were issued.  In her
view, his emails were harassing, intrusive, critical, and a testament to his
inability to co-parent.  The father maintains that the mother has refused to
communicate with him and has acted unilaterally.  He says she has breached many
provisions of the final Order in ways that interfere with his relationship with
his daughters.  He believes she imposes unnecessary restrictions on him that
have given rise to much of the conflict.

[
6
]

The parties had entered into two without
prejudice temporary agreements with respect to support, the first as of July
2007. The respondent had been paying support since March 2009 based on his
“self-stated imputed income” of $85,000 annually. In November 2010 a final Order
addressing child and spousal support was drafted.  It was approved by the
respondent’s counsel, but it was never issued.  The amounts paid were $950 per
month for spousal support and $1,226 per month for child support.  The draft
final Order carried these amounts forward and stipulated that there would be a
review in March 2012 so that the applicant could complete the education program
she had already embarked upon.

[
7
]

It is the respondent’s position that this Order
was not issued through inadvertence, and should be treated as an issued final Order.
The applicant says she did not understand this to be a final agreement as to
support; rather, she thought it was temporary until the respondent’s Canada Revenue
Agency (“CRA”) audit was complete so that his income could actually be
determined.

[
8
]

The applicant completed the program she was
taking at Algonquin College.  She has not become self-supporting.  In fact, she
has had very little employment since the separation.  For the past two years,
she has operated a gluten free baking business from her home.  She had a small
loss the first year and is showing a very small profit for the first nine
months of this year.  She has also obtained a part-time teaching position at
Algonquin College for the current term only.  She is paid $45 per hour for
between 4 to 6 hours per week.  As of January, she will be a tutor or teaching
assistant at the College and will work similar hours but for $25 per hour.  A
full-time position is opening up in September 2014.  She hopes to get it or at
least another teaching position at a partial load.  Either way, she would make
more than she is making now, but she did not say what the income for either
position would actually be.

[
9
]

The respondent maintains that the applicant is
seriously underemployed.  He asks the court to impute income of $50,000 per
annum to her. He seeks an Order that no spousal support should be paid, or in
the alternative for an award below the Spousal Support Advisory Guideline (“SSAG”)
range for a minimal further duration only.  He proposes to pay child support in
the set-off amount.

[
10
]

The CRA audit has been completed.  CRA
reassessed the father’s income for the years 2007, 2008 and 2009, at $455,646,
$492,928, and $791,130 respectively.  The father has filed a Notice of Objection.
He says his income is much lower; he has a huge debt load and other children
to support.  The father seeks to pay less than the table amount of child
support on the basis of undue hardship.  The applicant seeks retroactive child
and spousal support in amounts consistent with the audit, resulting in a claim
for arrears in the range of one million dollars.

Sole or joint decision making authority

[
11
]

There was no dispute as to whether a material
change in circumstances had occurred with reference to para. 1 of the final
Order where it stated there shall be no formal order as to the custody of the
children.  Each parent sought a change to that paragraph to award sole custody
to him or her.

[
12
]

The applicant testified the separation occurred
because the respondent became very demanding, jealous, and controlling of her.  She
says he physically assaulted her by grabbing her wrists, throwing her on the
bed and screaming at her.  She testified that he threatened to move to Toronto
with the children and that she would never see them again, after which she took
the girls and went to her sister’s.  The respondent broke into the house.  The
police were called and charges were laid against him.  He was convicted of
assaulting her and was subject to a peace bond.  In the result, the applicant has
been reluctant to deal directly with the respondent.

[
13
]

This start to the separation was inauspicious.  It
was not fertile ground for joint parental decision making.

[
14
]

Although she maintains the parenting
relationship was conflicted from the beginning of the separation, the mother
says she agreed to settle the first court case without an Order for custody
because she hoped the parenting co-ordinator and the counselling for the
children would bring about an improvement.  It is very clear these parents
required the help of a parenting co-ordinator.  This was an important term of their
consent final Order.  Although the parties had agreed to a named parenting
co-coordinator the respondent insisted on a number of revisions to the
co-ordinator’s standard form retainer agreement such that she declined to take the
case.  Then, although other individuals were suggested and names exchanged
between the parents, the respondent admitted in testimony that he was reluctant
to agree to anyone else because he felt the applicant had misrepresented him to
the social worker they had initially agreed would provide counselling for the children.
She may have done so; if so, that was corrected by retaining an alternate
counsellor.  In my view, the father’s explanation did not also justify failing
to move forward on retaining a much needed parenting co-coordinator.

[
15
]

It was the inability to implement the parenting
co-ordination term of the final Order that caused the case to come back to
court in the summer of 2011.  Even during the short break in the litigation
between November 2010 and June 2011, lawyers remained involved with respect to
the implementation of the Order.

[
16
]

Another term of the final Order limited the
exchange of emails to two brief emails each week, barring exceptional
circumstances.  This was also an important term of the final Order.  Reduction
in the number, length and tone of the emails was essential to reduce conflict
between the parents.  This term went hand in hand with the parenting co-ordination
provision.  The applicant points to the volume of emails she has received from
the respondent which, to her mind, were filled with recriminations, threats,
and attempts to control what she fed the children, how she dressed them, criticizing
her parenting as well as ongoing issues with respect to scheduling conflicts.

[
17
]

The applicant described other emails from the
respondent wherein he referred to the ongoing litigation between them, telling
her she was going to lose, he was going to get full custody, and she would end
up with less money than he was already paying her.  She requested numerous
times through counsel that he comply with the two emails per week limit, to no
avail.

[
18
]

The respondent defends the frequency and length
of his emails by saying the applicant was not responding to his reasonable
requests so he had to ask her repeatedly and send her reminders.  He attributes
the tone and content of certain emails to his frustration.  He testified that
he regretted some of the emails and apologized in court for some of them.

[
19
]

I have reviewed the emails tendered as Exhibits.
I find that the respondent was in clear breach of the court Order with respect
to the number and content of emails.  In general, his email communications to
the applicant show his criticism of and disrespect for her.  He reveals the
extent of his disagreements with her and her conduct.  On occasion, he is petty
and repeats long lists of historical grievances against the applicant.  He
accuses her of lying to the children, not being honest with her lawyer, and
stupidly running up costs.  He threatens her by asking what would happen if the
health department found out she was running a home-based commercial kitchen.  He
criticizes her for allowing the children to play with two other children who he
believes made an unsuitable comment about Princess Diana.  These emails are not
indicative of an ability to cooperate, communicate civilly or to co-parent.

[
20
]

By way of one example, on April 21, 2012, the
respondent delivered a four page email to the applicant which included these
remarks:  “…it must bug the crap out of you, I remarried a younger, smart,
educated and attractive woman…even more so we have had kids….maybe you have an
issue with money we spend or make, we are entitled to spend money as long as we
don’t deny Laila and Maya of anything….we can see it bugs you we travel, … also
the new house we purchased seems to bother you…”.  The lack of civility is
clear.

[
21
]

The respondent blatantly refused to comply with
the restrictions on emails imposed by the final Order.  On April 25, 2012, he
responded to the complaint about the length and tone of his previous email:
“Did you by chance listen to the priest’s sermon on Sunday and the message he has
about healing and filling your heart with love? …No one is taunting you, we are
pointing out the obvious, sorry you or [your lawyers] do not like the truth….I
am sorry if you’re annoyed by my email(s) and take it to your lawyer, frankly
it does not [phase] me and I have no problem defending it with a judge or
whoever. What am I going to say, everything I have stated is 100% true, so be
it.”

[
22
]

The respondent also resorted to threats in some
of his communications to the applicant.  At least two emails in 2012 threatened
to report her to the criminal defence lawyer he had retained and to notify the
Ottawa Police Service if a third party who assisted the applicant was at the
exchange

or he was required to pick up the children at her sister’s
house in accordance with the court Order.  The respondent maintained this would
be criminal harassment under the
Criminal Code
.

[
23
]

More recently, in February 2013, the respondent
wrote to the applicant his opinion that he would do very well in court but she
would have to justify more than 75 complaints which he then went on to list.

[
24
]

In January 2013, the respondent emailed the
applicant about her “bizarre behaviour”, told her she was “spiralling downward”
and if she did not “get [her] act together as it relates to our kids”, he would
“be seeking some sort of assessment”.  Again in May 2013, he wrote that if
there was no settlement soon, he would bring “a motion to have a full
assessment of your mental mind and health examined (prior to trial) based on the
very disturbing behaviours you continue to demonstrate”.

[
25
]

I find that the respondent was unwilling to
comply with the email restrictions imposed by the final Order.  I find that he
was unwilling to comply with the requirement of that Order to retain a
parenting co-ordinator.  I find compliance with both of these terms was
essential for the final Order to have a realistic chance to succeed given it
did not designate legal custodial decision making authority.  I accept the
applicant’s testimony that in her own mind, the inclusion of these terms was
the reason why she settled the previous litigation without seeking a specific Order
for sole custody.

[
26
]

The applicant also received two letters from a
prominent criminal defence lawyer retained by the respondent, cautioning her
about her behaviour towards the respondent and drawing provisions of the
Criminal
Code
to her attention.  She found these letters to be inexplicable in terms
of anything she had done, and intimidating.  The respondent referred to this
lawyer and the potential for criminal prosecution in subsequent emails to the
applicant.  He also had criminal defence lawyers write to both of her sisters
in similar vein.

[
27
]

I will not comment on the intentions or knowledge
of the lawyer(s), who were not witnesses at trial, but I find the respondent
clearly intended these letters to intimidate the applicant in the course of
their custody litigation.

[
28
]

For his part, the respondent believes that the
applicant never intended to adhere to the terms of the final Order.  He says
she breached the Order early on, and frequently thereafter.  The first alleged
breach is an email the applicant sent to the proposed counsellor for the
children, setting out her concerns in relation to the respondent and the
children, and why she felt the children required counselling.  The respondent saw
this as a breach of the Order which prescribed confidential counselling for the
children, and of the parenting principle which restrained the parents from
disparaging each other to or in the presence of the children.  It is not
necessary for me to determine the accuracy of the contents of this email.  I do
find that it did not breach either provision.

[
29
]

The next alleged breach was of the requirement
for the applicant to apply for the children’s passports on an expedited basis
because the respondent was taking them out of the country later in December
2010.  She did apply promptly but relied on information from the passport
office that the passports would be ready in time without the need to expedite
them.  This proved to be the case.  Despite this and the fact it happened more
than three years ago, the respondent wanted the court to find the applicant in
breach of the Order because she had not in fact expedited the passports.  He
submitted this revealed her intention not to adhere to the final Order.  I am
not persuaded of this conclusion on balance on probabilities.

[
30
]

The final Order provided that if the pickups and
drop offs could not take place at school, they would take place at the mother’s
house or other location designated by her.  She has never felt comfortable
having the respondent at her home and has always designated another location.
Initially, this was her sister’s home.  After the final Order, this sister moved
to an address farther away from the father’s home.  He then refused to go to
her house.  The mother selected the parking lot of the children’s school.  She
also arranged for a third party, Ms. Nagora, to handle the exchanges, rather
than to be present herself.

[
31
]

The respondent submits that because the Order
mentions the mother’s home first, it requires the transitions to take place
there in the first instance.  I disagree.  The Order gives the mother the
choice of her home or another location she designates.  The father could hardly
have been surprised that she did designate another location given that the
exchanges prior to the final Order had taken place at her sister’s home.  The
respondent also disagrees that there ought to be any third party present for
the transitions of the children.  The final Order does not require or preclude
third party transitions.  Having a third party handle the transitions is not a
breach of the court Order.

[
32
]

Before the transitions moved to the school
parking lot on a regular basis, an unfortunate incident took place on Good
Friday, April 2011.  The applicant designated her sister’s home as the place of
the exchange.  The father would not go there. They agreed on the school parking
lot.  The father and his wife arrived with the children.  The applicant’s
sister was already there.  The father walked the children towards their aunt,
carrying their bag.  Something happened during the transfer of the bag and
words erupted.  The aunt “dropped the F bomb” as the respondent puts it, in the
hearing of the children.  He was very offended.  The aunt felt the father assaulted
her while transferring the bag to her.  Later, she called the police to
complain.  No charges were laid.  The father maintained he did nothing wrong.  In
his opinion, she was trying to create trouble for him.  Despite mentioning in
court and in his emails that he had a complete video recording of this event,
it was not produced at trial.

[
33
]

After this, the applicant’s sister did not
participate in transitioning the children.

[
34
]

The respondent does not object to Ms. Nagora
per
se
.  Rather he objects to the concept of having a third party present for
transitions. There has been one occasion when he waited ten minutes for Ms.
Nagora and the children at the school, and then went to her house (which is
nearby) where he did pick up the girls. In general the presence of Ms. Nagora
has not occasioned problems in the transitioning of the children between
parents.

[
35
]

The respondent has not established any breach or
denial of his residential access time by the applicant in relation to her
designation of the transition point or involvement of a third party at
transitions.

[
36
]

The respondent also alleged the applicant was in
breach of paras. 16 and 17 of the final Order.  These paragraphs state:

Information Held by Third Parties.
The Respondent shall be entitled to independently discuss the children’s
health, wellbeing and ongoing needs with the children’s health care
provider(s), dentist, orthodontist, teacher(s), coach (es), counsellor(s) and
any other professional(s) involved in their lives from time to time.

The Respondent shall be entitled
to access to the children’s school records (including report cards), health
care records and activity schedules.  The parties shall provide to one another
copies of the children’s report cards, important records and assessment results
relating to the children’s health and/or education as soon as possible after
the documentation is received.

[
37
]

The respondent alleges a breach in that the
applicant does not provide him advance notice of children’s appointments.  The
terms of the Order do not require advance notice to be given.  He also alleges
she has failed to provide copies of everything she received pertaining to the
children.  She did provide the respondent with copies of report cards,
important records, and assessment results.  The respondent also alleges the
applicant did not provide him with sufficient information from third party
service providers.  She did provide him with brief updates on the children as required
by para. 18 of the Order (the email provision).  The fact that he wanted more
information does not put her in breach of the Order.  Each individual parent
may contact a service provider for additional information.

[
38
]

The respondent did establish that there were
some forms and notices from the school, not enumerated in para. 17, that the applicant
did not send over to him.  Eventually in September 2013 he asked the school to copy
him directly; the school readily complied.

[
39
]

The parents have disagreed about medical
treatment.  A paediatrician recommended Laila should have blood tests and be
seen at the Children’s Hospital of Eastern Ontario (“CHEO”). The respondent refused
permission based on his misreading of the paediatrician’s letter.  The
respondent contacted the family doctor to object and instructed the applicant
to cancel the appointment.  Lawyer’s letters were exchanged over a six week
period.  The respondent then changed his mind after re-reading the letter.

[
40
]

The respondent complained that the applicant did
not notify him in advance of medical appointments for the children, only after
the fact.  The applicant admits this.  She points to the above example in
explanation of why she does not want to.  Although it is not required by the
court Order, I find both parents should know in advance of upcoming
appointments for the children so that each may provide their own observations
and input to physicians.  What should not happen is that an upcoming or
proposed medical appointment becomes an occasion of prolonged controversy
between the parents.

[
41
]

The mother has shown that Laila writes some of
her numbers and letters backwards.  Laila has required extra help in math and
spelling.  The applicant would like to have Laila tested for dyslexia and
attention deficit disorder.  Her concerns arise from her observation that Laila
is quite active, has difficulty sitting still, and focussing in some
situations. Laila has had some issues with chewing her hair, her clothing and
pencils, with not being able to sit still, and with focussing.  This has been
observed at school and by both parents. But there is no recommendation from the
school that Laila undergo attention deficit testing.  The respondent disagrees
that Laila should be tested.  He thinks it is unnecessary.

[
42
]

The applicant discussed her concerns with the
children’s doctor.  The doctor sent out a brief questionnaire called a “Snap
Test” to be completed by the parents, teachers, and choir director, summarizing
their own observations of Laila.  The purpose of the Snap Test was to provide
additional information to the doctor to assist him in determining whether
anything further should be done from a medical standpoint.  The test is a one
page check box form.

[
43
]

The respondent refused to complete the test.  He
forbade the teachers from doing so.  He intervened with the choir director who
had already filled it out.  By the father’s actions, the doctor did not receive
the feedback which may have enabled him to make an informed recommendation
sufficient to resolve the parents’ disagreement and ensure Laila’s needs were
met.

[
44
]

The parents also debated the necessity of a
puffer and allergy testing for Laila.

[
45
]

The respondent supports extra homework for Laila
to bring up her level in math, spelling and grammar.  He prepared extra work
for her to do and shared the materials with the mother.  The mother did
participate yet this also attracted disapproval from the father.  Emails dated
in May, June and October 2013 were tendered in which he set out inadequacies in
how the mother was doing the extra homework with Laila.  The applicant
responded, explaining her reason for not having Laila correct each error at the
time it was made; she wanted to see a picture over time of where her main areas
of difficulty were.  The respondent rejected this explanation with a nine line statement
of why she should do it his way.  In an email to the mother dated October 25,
2013, the respondent included eight paragraphs criticizing her homework efforts
with the girls.

[
46
]

The parents have different religious faiths.
The mother is Catholic.  The father is Muslim.  The parents agreed to baptize
the children in the Catholic faith.  They also agreed the children would attend
Catholic schools.  Despite these agreements, disagreements have arisen. The
father has asked the mother not to serve pork to the children.  She regards
this as undue interference in her household.  She has fed them pork but says
the girls refuse it now in any event.

[
47
]

Now, the father has the children join him when
he is observing religious days by fasting.  He explains they want to share in
his observance with him.  The mother describes this in an email to the father as
him “withholding food and water” from the children.

[
48
]

The law is clear both parents may engage their
children in their individual faith-based practises while the children are
residing with them, as long as so doing is not contrary to the children’s best
interests and does not expose them to danger.  Daytime fasting during the days
the children are with the father in the month leading up to Eid would not
constitute a dangerous situation for these children.  Further, the father does
not make this obligatory for the children.

[
49
]

I find the applicant could easily have respected
the respondent’s wish that she not serve pork to the children, while still
providing them a balanced diet.  I find her description of the children’s
participation in his religious observance of fasting to be intentionally
provocative.

[
50
]

The respondent asks the court to order the
applicant to comply with a specific dietary practise. In
Rosenberg v.
Minster
,
2011 ONSC 4758
, 11 R.F.L. (7th) 236 (Ont. S.C.), the court dealt
with a similar request at paras. 11, 17 and 19:

The best interests of a child
usually means that a child's relationship with the other parent is more
important than exclusive conformity with the religious practices of one parent.

H. (B.) v. Z. (S.) supra
citing
Young v. Young
(1993),
1993 CanLII 34 (SCC)
, 49 R.F.L.
(3d) 117 (S.C.C.). At page 120 of
Young v. Young
, the court held that

The custodial parent does not have
the right to determine whether limits should be placed on access. His or her
obligation to make basic child-rearing decisions does not mean that an access
parent of a different faith should not share his or her religion with a child.

…Section 6(4) of the late
Professor McLeod's signature publication,
Child Custody Law and Practice

is a compelling summary of the fundamental principal of religious tolerance
within Canadian Law. This principal has been compellingly articulated
throughout every line of the court's work. Within family law, the principal is
soundly settled: the court will only encroach upon the personal domain of
religious freedom, if the failure to do so is shown to place a child at
substantial risk of harm.

…In my view, there is no evidence
that the father's manner of caring for and feeding Chayala will place her at
any risk whatsoever. The respondent mother's motion that the applicant father
comply with Jewish dietary laws during his access visits with his daughter is
dismissed.

[
51
]

Accordingly no order will be made in this
regard.

[
52
]

The record shows some co-operation and flexibility
between the parents.  But overall, they are polar opposites and do not connect
as parents.

[
53
]

Both parents seek sole legal custody.  They both
point to their perception of the other’s contribution to the ongoing conflict
in support of their claim.  The applicant also relies on the fact that she has
been the primary residential parent throughout.  She submits the evidence shows
the respondent does not respect her as a parent or communicate with her in a
civil, constructive manner.  The respondent seeks sole custody to prevent the
applicant from cutting him out of the children’s lives.  He worries that if she
had sole legal custody, she may use her decision making authority to
marginalize him as a parent.  He believes the applicant has shown herself
unwilling to share information with him, whereas he is more than willing to do
so.  Alternatively, the father requests parallel parenting, which is a form of
joint custody.  He did not plead this, but raised it as an option in his
testimony and closing submissions.

[
54
]

In
Kaplanis v. Kaplanis
(2005),
2005 CanLII 1625 (ON CA)
, 10 R.F.L.
(6th) 373 (Ont. C.A.), the Ontario Court of Appeal overturned an award of joint
custody where there was no evidence of historical cooperation and appropriate communication
between the parents, only the hope of improvement.  Here, there is not only an
inauspicious history between the parents; the respondent has thwarted the
mechanisms put in place in the final Order in 2010 that might have assisted the
parents to improve their communication and to gain an ability to parent
cooperatively.

[
55
]

Joint or parallel joint custody have been
awarded where necessary to protect a parent–child relationship from
encroachment by the other parent.  This was the case in
Andrade v. Kennelly

(2006),
2006 CanLII 20845 (ON SC)
, 33 R.F.L. (6th) 125 (Ont. S.C.), aff’d
2007 ONCA 898
, 46 R.F.L. (6th)
235 (Ont. C.A.) where the trial judge found that the mother would not support
the relationship between children and father because she held the erroneous
view that he was mentally ill and dangerous to the children.  Here it is the
respondent who questions the applicant’s mental health and stability without
evidentiary foundation.

[
56
]

The respondent submits that the applicant
engages in alienating behaviour and that this is a primary reason why he should
have sole or joint custody.  His counsel directed me to
A.G.L. v. K.B.D.

(2009),
2009 CanLII 943 (ON SC)
, 65 R.F.L. (6th) 146 (Ont. S.C.), where the court referred to “
Pathological
Alienation: Warning Signs of Behaviours Exhibited by Child, Alienating parent
and Rejected parent

The applicant retained Dave Clarke, CPA, CA, CBV

2011 and 2012 for the purpose of establishing child and spousal support

Mr. Clarke used a net worth approach to
calculate the income available to the respondent. He said this approach is used
where a taxpayer’s spending is greater than the taxpayer’s declared income. It

attributable to a taxpayer and the income declared on the taxpayer’s income tax
returns. Where the cash outflows are greater than the income reported on the
income tax return and a source of funds cannot be identified, the difference is
considered to be unreported income.   Any such amounts would then be grossed up
to show what would have to have been earned before income taxes in order to
produce the amount of unreported income net after tax.  The grossed up amount
was added to the respondent’s declared income as imputed income.

for the three young children of his current marriage.

The respondent has valued his Merrickville vacant

]

The minimum expenses claimed by the respondent,
for his three real properties, his child and spousal support payments, gifts to

]

CRA reassessed the respondent’s income for 2007,

]

The applicant submitted the CRA reassessment
figures should be taken as
prima facie
evidence of the respondent’s
income.  I disagree.  I do not have the foundational information upon which CRA

[
137
]

The respondent’s personal income tax returns for
2010, 2011 and 2012 report total income of $136,374, $104,995 and $174,878
respectively.  He predicts he will earn $123,640 in 2013.

[
138
]

I find the respondent’s income as declared on his
income tax returns is not an accurate reflection of income available to him for
the purpose of establishing child and spousal support. This conclusion is
derived from Mr. Clarke’s opinion evidence, from the fact of the outcome of the
CRA audit which resulted in income reassessments which are markedly different
from the respondent’s declared income, and from the respondent’s own financial
statements and testimony.   The information the respondent and his bookkeeper
put before the court paints a clear picture of insolvency yet he states he
intends to continue his business because it is the very best way he can provide
for his family. He used colourful language to describe the hard work ahead to
chip away at his debt, comparing it to “using a teaspoon to fill a crater”.

[
139
]

Despite this description, the respondent asked
for one to two years to get his affairs in order. He asked to have his income
capped at $135,000 for that duration, despite what he might actually earn,
saying he thought he could make things work with that number. I found no air of

[
140
]

The respondent has been operating this business
since 2001. He is not inexperienced nor is the business short lived.  His
explanation that he robs Peter to pay Paul to stay afloat seems implausible and

that a person in his self-described financial circumstances could reasonably be
expected to take.

[
141
]

The law requires the respondent to establish his
income.  In fact he has made it extremely difficult for the court to determine
his income. He has intermingled his personal and business finances.  He has

provide Mr. Clarke with additional information prior to trial but chose not to.
The approach taken in cross-examination of Mr. Clarke was to highlight
information he did not have and assumptions he did make that may be incorrect,
but not to present the missing information or the allegedly accurate information
to him. No contrary opinion witness was tendered.  The respondent’s persistence

at the same time he paints it and himself as insolvent lead me to the

[
142
]

Based on the record before me I have determined
the respondent’s income for support purposes to range on average between

Spousal and Child Support

[
143
]

Although his pleading sought termination of
spousal support, at trial the respondent was less clear in his position. He
proposed a review Order to coincide with the completion of the objection
process from the CRA audit.  He submitted income should be imputed to the
applicant retroactively in the amount of $50,000 per annum. He stated he had
already been paying spousal support for 6 years on a relationship of 10 years
cohabitation.  He denied that the applicant had established any need beyond the
amount of $950 per month currently in pay.

[
144
]

The respondent also asked the court to conduct
the review that the November 2010 agreement stipulated should happen in March
2012, but at the same time did not seem to challenge the amount of $950 in
spousal support. He submitted the 2012 review should take into account that he
had paid more than he was legally required to pay in the years from the
separation up to 2012, but he also provided standard of living schedules to
demonstrate that he should have a reduction in child support due to undue
hardship in many of those years. The draft order he submitted continued to seek
as an alternative, a termination date for spousal support.

[
145
]

The applicant asks that child and spousal
support be retroactively increased back to the date of separation in amounts commensurate
with the CRA audit and the Clarke report. By her calculation the respondent
owes her arrears of child support in the amount of $362,574 and arrears of
spousal support in the amount of $827,057. From January 2014 forward she seeks
child support of $8,132 per month and spousal support of $16,800 per month
based on an imputed income of $687,300 for the respondent and an actual income
of $13,000 per annum for herself.

Retroactive Claim

[
146
]

S. (D.B.) v. G. (S.R.)

2006 SCC 37
deals
with retroactivity in child support but many of the principles enunciated there
also apply to spousal support. Here the claim is for both child and spousal
support to be adjusted to the income the court determines back to the date of
separation.  This is discretionary relief and requires the court to balance
competing factors in the exercise of its discretion. No one factor is decisive
on its own.

[
147
]

What is the explanation for the delay in
bringing the claim forward to court and is it reasonable? Did the recipient
make a voluntary and informed choice to accept the status quo payments over the
period in question? Absent a reasonable excuse, responsibility for uncorrected
deficiencies known to both recipient and payor may be attributable to both.

[
148
]

In this case the applicant entered into various
agreements at various points in time for child and spousal support payments.
She had legal advice. She was aware of the issues with respect to establishing
the respondent’s level of income. She did not actually seek a retroactive
adjustment to the date of separation until an amendment to her pleadings made
at trial.

[
149
]

Was there blameworthy conduct on the part of the
payor?  In this case there was blameworthy conduct by the respondent in failing
to correct the amount of income he had imputed to himself as the basis for the
November 2010 agreement, upon learning that his declared income for 2010 was
significantly higher.  This was compounded when subsequently he did not advise
the applicant of his reported incomes for 2011 or 2012, which also exceeded the
self-imputed amount. In this way he knowingly diminished his child support
obligation.  I would include in the category of blameworthy conduct his failure
to disclose the outcome of the CRA audit, promptly upon receipt in December
2012.

[
150
]

Next, the circumstances

of the children
and spouse should be considered. What was the impact upon them of the failure
to disclose the level of income actually reported to CRA?  The respondent was
paying child support for the two children of $1226 per month. Based on the
incomes he reported to CRA the child support should have been $1854 per month
in 2010, $1477 per month in 2011, and $2297 per month in 2012. Over the period
of the separation the applicant has incurred debt. In addition to her mortgage
she owes approximately $92,000, which includes $40,000 for legal fees. Her
financial statement shows a negative net worth. The applicant’s liquid assets
total $614 in a bank account. She has depleted her RRSP account by $52,533
since separation.

[
151
]

The court should also consider the hardship to
the payor occasioned by making a retroactive award.

Generally speaking

a

retroactive award disrupts a payor’s management of his financial
affairs in a way a prospective award does not. To the extent the agreements
made between these parties were made with fair disclosure, the respondent has a
valid reliance interest in them. For the reasons already given as to the
respondent’s actual income for support purposes, and comments directed towards
his financial statement, it is difficult to assess the actual impact a
retroactive order would have on him.

[
152
]

It is in my view important to distinguish the
consequences in terms of retroactivity that should properly flow from the
respondent’s failure to disclose his actual as declared income in 2010, 2011
and 2012, from his failure to make prompt disclosure of the CRA reassessment
notices received in December 2012 with respect to 2007 to 2009. Having
underestimated his income in the 2010 agreement, it was incumbent upon him to
correct the error forthwith. Weight to be given to any hardship to the
respondent arising from a retroactive order to clean up his own non-disclosure
is slight.

[
153
]

The CRA reassessments in my view are different.
They do not apply directly to years in issue. Unlike declared income their
impact on support would not have been immediately known, other than to know
that controversy and debate would have ensued. They led the applicant to retain
an expert to determine the respondent’s income, which report was not available
until 2013. In my view more weight would have to be given to hardship on the
respondent’s side in coming up with a retroactive payment derived at least in
this way from the CRA reassessments.

[
154
]

The court must also determine the date of
retroactivity.

There are a number of choices available:  the application
date, the date formal notice of the claim was given, the date effective notice
of the claim was given, and the date when support should have increased. The
Supreme Court of Canada has adopted the date of effective notice as the general
rule.

[
155
]

In this case the application was issued in July
2012.  That document claimed retroactivity to 2009. Formal notice of the full
extent of the retroactive claim was given at trial. The November 2010 agreement
was made with knowledge the CRA audit was pending, and that there was
uncertainty surrounding the respondent’s income, but without specific reservation
of a right to seek a retroactive adjustment dependant on the outcome of the CRA
audit.  On the other hand had the respondent disclosed the income he actually
declared to CRA in a timely way one expects the support would have been
immediately adjusted.

[
156
]

I have considered whether I should retroactively
change the support that was paid first voluntarily and then by signed agreement
prior to November 2010. So doing would amount to a retroactive period of five
years, between the date of separation and date of issuance of the application
in 2012. From August 2007 to February 2009 the respondent paid unallocated
support i.e. non tax deductible support of $3,500 per month. This full amount
has not been factored in to the applicant’s summary of arrears. Nor has a
calculation been prepared to show what the positions of the parties would have
been had this payment been appropriately allocated between child and spousal
support. I have only one financial statement signed during these years and it is
by the applicant, dated March 19, 2008. It shows a monthly surplus of
$1,701.80. It is extremely difficult to assess quantum of spousal support on
the record of evidence I have for the years prior to November 2010.

[
157
]

The parties’ retroactive claims also suffer from
on the one hand, asking the court to accept the respondent’s declared incomes
in those years as accurate, despite the CRA reassessments, and on the other
hand, from asking the court to simply accept the CRA reassessments as accurate
on their face and in the absence of CRA’s foundational documents or any expert
opinion related to those years.

[
158
]

For better or worse, the parties were prepared
to enter into a final order for support in November 2010, subject to a material
change of circumstances and a review in March 2012, knowing the respondent was
being audited by CRA for the years 2007-2009.

[
159
]

For all of these reasons, I decline to make a
retroactive order for the period of time prior to the agreement for a final
order made in November 2010.

[
160
]

I have no hesitation in finding that child
support should be retroactively adjusted from November 1, 2010 forward, based
on the respondent’s declared income for the year 2010, and based on the income
I have determined him to have had, for 2011 and 2012.
[1]
By my calculation the
arrears for child support after credit is given for amounts paid total $58,424.

[
161
]

I have taken a different approach to spousal
support in view of my finding that some weight should be given to the agreement
reached in November 2010 as it relates to spousal support. The agreement
recorded that the respondent was paying spousal support beyond the guideline
amount for his self-imputed income of $85,000. It also provided for a review of

[
162
]

As noted the income the respondent self-imputed
to himself of $85,000 formed the basis of the agreement, and was inaccurate.

[
163
]

I also want to give some effect to the agreement
for a review in March 2012. At that point the education program was complete

[
164
]

For these reasons, in giving some effect to the
parties agreement, and in weighing the impact of retroactivity on both parties,
I have decided to award high end SSAG spousal support based on declared incomes

[
165
]

Why did I not use the incomes I determined the
respondent to have had for 2011 and 2012 for this purpose? I have tried to

would have or ought to have addressed them at the time. The CRA reassessments

only available after the agreed upon March 2012 review should have been
conducted and would not have been known to the parties at that time. I reached
the conclusion that income should be imputed to the applicant as of January
2013, but not before that date. All of these considerations combined in my
decision to approach this period of arrears as I did, knowing that others may
have approached it differently. For example, a higher retroactive award for
spousal support based on the respondent’s deemed income would be more difficult
for him to pay than a prospective award, and may well have warranted a final
termination date not necessarily appropriate to arise from a retroactive award

[
166
]

The respondent shall pay to the applicant the
sum of $97,898 with no income tax consequences on account of arrears of child
and support I have created by this award, for the period between November 2010
to the conclusion of 2012.

Prospective Support

[
167
]

What I loosely term the” prospective” portion of
my support award shall commence as of January 1, 2013. This award will reflect

[
168
]

Using the midpoint of $290,000 for the
respondent I order him to pay to the applicant $3,608 per month child support

169
]

Using $36,000 annual income for the applicant,
the SSAG range is $4,886 at the low end to $6431 at the high end.  Using

should be below the low end of the SSAG in recognition of his high debt load

[
171
]

Based on the respondent’s imputed income,
combined with his spouse’s gross income, they would not be able to cover their

[
172
]

On the other hand  and as I have previously
found, the respondent’s budget also includes  expenses of some $6400 per month
to carry a lot in Manotick and a rental property, which is either vacant now or
soon to become vacant based upon his evidence at trial. In my view it is
incumbent upon the respondent to dispose of these properties. Whether he does
so or not, he cannot rely upon these expenses in reduction of his spousal
support obligation to the applicant. There are also other reductions open to
him, including reducing the $2,500 per month shown for a nanny.

[
173
]

I agree with the respondent that the applicant
has not demonstrated a need for spousal support within the SSAG range and that
he cannot pay support in that range and still meet his other reasonable
expenses. At the same time, the applicant has primary residential custody of
their children, and there are steps available to the respondent to reduce many
of his expenses.

[
174
]

Although this is not technically a review or
variation given that my award will be the first final order made, the parties
had previously agreed to spousal support of $950 per month, they have now been
separated for seven years after ten years of cohabitation, and the respondent
has paid spousal support for the entire period of separation.  The property
settlement they reached in 2007 was modest.  The respondent’s declared incomes
in 2004 to 2007 were also modest, ranging from $35,000 to $55,000, the latter
year having been subject to re-assessment by CRA. Despite the questions about
his declared income I find it likely he has enjoyed a post- separation increase
in income. He has re-partnered and has another family.

[
175
]

In my view, these are circumstances where the
SSAG should be approached with caution. This is not a case where a support
recipient can reasonably assume the spousal support award will automatically
fall within the SSAG range, especially when the recipient’s financial statement
does not approach that level of need. Neither counsel assisted me with any case
law where the SSAG had been applied in similar circumstances.

[
176
]

I have concluded that spousal support shall be
paid in the amount of $1400 per month for 2013 and in the amount of $1000 per
month for 2014, until further order of this court. Credit shall be given for
amounts paid.

[
177
]

The respondent did submit that any spousal
support award should be subject to a final termination date. He provided a case
where spousal support was terminated where the cohabitation was of similar
duration and the couple also had two children of similar ages to the case at
bar. However, in that case the claimant spouse had obtained permanent
employment and the court also ordered equal residential custody of the children.
Those are not the facts here.

[
178
]

The SSAG with child support formula is
indefinite subject to review or change in the event of a material change in
circumstances.  Given the length of this cohabitation and the age and education
of the applicant it does seem unlikely that spousal support will continue until
the youngest child completes high school. However, the applicant is not yet
fully employed and her actual income from full employment has yet to be
established. I find that the applicant may well have increased income as of
September 2014 having regard to upcoming opportunities at Algonquin College. She
shall be required to disclose to the respondent when she has obtained full time
employment or an annual earned income of $60,000, (her estimate of what she
might earn through full employment at Algonquin College).  Either event shall
entitle the respondent to seek a review of spousal support.  In addition
spousal support may also be reviewed in May 2017 (ten years after separation),
to determine whether entitlement to ongoing spousal support still exists.

Respondent’s hardship claim

[
179
]

The respondent sought to pay a lesser amount for
child support than prescribed by the
CSG
based on a claim for an undue
hardship. He admits his household is at a higher standard of living than the applicant’s
in 2012 having regard to his declared income. He did not provide a standard of
living schedule for subsequent years. He claims he would have been at a lower
standard of living for 2010 and 2011 had he paid support for those years based
on his declared income.

[
180
]

Section 10(1) and (2) of the
CSG
provides
as follows:

Section
10: Undue Hardship

(1)

On either spouse’s application, a court may award an amount of child
support that is different from the amount determined under any of sections 3 to
5, 8 or 9 if the court finds that the spouse making the request, or a child in
respect of whom the request is made, would otherwise suffer undue hardship.

(2)

Circumstances that may cause a spouse or child to suffer undue hardship
include the following:

(a)

The spouse has the responsibility for an
unusually high  level of debts reasonably incurred to support the spouses and
their children prior to the separation or to earn a living;

(b)

The spouse has unusually high expenses in
relation to exercising access to a child;

(c)

The spouse has a legal duty under a judgment,
order or written separation agreement to support any person;

(d)

The spouse has a legal duty to support a child,
other than a child of the marriage, who is:

(i)

Under the age of majority, or

(ii)

The age of majority or over but is unable, by
reason of illness, disability  or other cause, to obtain the necessities of
life; and

(e)

The spouse has a legal duty to support any
person who is unable to obtain the necessities of life due to an illness or
disability.

[
181
]

I decline to exercise my discretion to reduce
child support payments for Laila and Maya in 2010, in which year I have only
increased two months of child support. For 2011, the respondent relies on his
payment of child support for his two children of his first marriage as giving
rise to the undue hardship. But, I do not know the date of the birth of the
oldest child. He would have turned 18 at some point in 2011 given that he was
said to be 20 in December 2013. Was he still entitled to child support
thereafter? When did he move in with his father? The respondent has not
established these facts.

[
182
]

He relies on his debt level but has not taken
reasonable steps to dispose of real properties in order to reduce those
expenses. The payments he makes to his parents are not pursuant to a legal
obligation.

[
183
]

This claim is dismissed.

Total
Arrears of support/overall assessment of support order

[
184
]

The awards made for child and spousal support
create arrears. By my calculation I have required the respondent to pay $138,388
in arrears that have no tax consequences. The arrears created by my award for
spousal support which commences January 1, 2013 will be tax includable and tax
deductible.  The amount owing is $5650 with tax consequences.

[
185
]

Before finalizing my decision I have considered
this outcome in relation to all of the facts of the case. These include, but
are not limited to the duration of the relationship, the ages of the spouses at
separation, their child care obligations, retraining obligations, the duration
of the support to date and ongoing duration as yet unknown, their needs and
means, and the financial impact on the applicant and children in her care
during the period covered by the retroactive claim.

[
186
]

Overall, I find that the retroactive and
prospective awards of child and spousal support are fair and reasonable, and
balanced between the parties and their needs and means in the years in
question. As a final measure I have considered the outcome in relation to the
knowledge that I could have analyzed the claim for retroactive spousal support
by reference to the higher incomes determined for the respondent in 2011 and
2012 and declined to do so for reasons given. I simply wish to state here that
having reached the conclusions I did reach; having reviewed them again in light
of the overall outcome achieved, I am satisfied the outcome is appropriate.
